products.name: Adjudica
products.tagline: Rank anything by comparing two things at a time
products.description:
Deciding what you actually prefer out of forty things is hard. Deciding which of two things you prefer is easy. Adjudica turns the first problem into a lot of the second one, and keeps an ELO rating for every item as you go.

Import a list as text or a folder of photos, then answer pairs. Rankings are fairness-filtered rather than raw: confidence shrinkage pulls items with few comparisons toward the middle instead of letting one lucky win crown them, and outlier dampening stops a single strange judgement from dominating. Fair, Raw and 0-100 views are all available, because which one is honest depends on how far through you are.

Groupings let you start a new trial from a set of photos, clone an existing one with or without carrying scores over, or extend one with new entrants. Items can be edited mid-trial without discarding the comparisons already made.

products.name: BreachRadar
products.tagline: Breach monitoring and an outreach queue, on your own machine
products.description:
Watches SEC EDGAR 8-K Item 1.05 filings and six incident-press feeds, and puts every new disclosure in front of you as a triage queue rather than a dashboard you have to remember to open.

Eight columns from Inbox to Call booked. The day counter on each card is computed as it renders, so a target sitting in Hold turns colour by itself on the morning it enters the window you care about. Nothing is auto-filed into an outbound column — extracting an organisation from a headline is a heuristic and it is wrong often enough to matter.

No daemon, no API keys, no telemetry and no server. It polls when you open it, or once a day at most. Your board, notes and settings stay in a folder in your home directory and an update never touches them.

macos.notes:
# Breach Radar 0.3.2

A packaging fix. If you already have 0.3.1 running, nothing about the app
changes — but 0.3.1 could not be installed by anyone who downloaded it, so it
should not be passed on.

**Downloads open properly again.** The 0.3.1 bundle was signed before the
database CLI was copied into it, which invalidates the signature. That is
invisible on the machine that built the app — a local build carries no
quarantine flag, so macOS never checks — and fatal everywhere else: a
downloaded copy reports *"BreachRadar is damaged and can't be opened"*, which
right-click → Open cannot get past. The CLI is now copied in before signing,
and the build refuses to continue if the signature does not verify, so this
cannot ship again without someone noticing.

Downloading Breach Radar for the first time still shows the usual
*"unidentified developer"* prompt, because the app is signed ad-hoc rather than
with an Apple Developer ID. Right-click the app and choose **Open** to get past
that one; it is asked once, per machine.

Everything in 0.3.1 — per-contact claim codes, server-chosen subdomains, and
the move of your board to `~/.undercurrent/db/breachradar/` — is unchanged and
described in `NOTES-0.3.1.md`.

products.name: Depot
products.tagline: The storefront and updater for everything here
products.description:
Depot lists everything on this channel, installs it, and tells you when a newer version exists.

On Android it is the reason updates work at all: an APK installed by hand from a web page has nothing that ever checks for a successor, so Depot does the checking — once a day, in the background, with a notification naming what is behind. Nothing installs without you tapping it; no third-party store on Android can install silently, and one that claimed to would be lying.

On macOS it installs apps that have no updater of their own and updates the ones that do. It replaces a bundle atomically, so a crash halfway through cannot leave an app that will not start, and because Depot is not a browser the apps it installs carry no quarantine flag — the Gatekeeper prompt you get from a download never appears.

Every download is checked against its published SHA-256 and an Ed25519 signature from the release key before anything is installed. The public half of that key is compiled into Depot, so write access to the public release repository is not enough to push code to anybody.

macos.notes:
The first release of Depot — the storefront and updater for this channel.

**macOS**

- Lists every product the channel publishes for macOS, with what you have
  installed next to what is available.
- Installs and updates apps that have no updater of their own. The bundle is
  replaced atomically, so a crash halfway through cannot leave an app that will
  not start, and a running copy is quit first rather than having its files pulled
  out from under it.
- Apps it installs carry **no quarantine flag**, because Depot is not a browser.
  The Gatekeeper prompt you meet once on a downloaded app never appears for
  anything installed this way.
- Writes to `/Applications` when that is writable by your account, which it is on
  a stock macOS, and falls back to `~/Applications`. It never asks for an
  administrator password: an installer that can elevate is a much larger thing to
  trust than one that cannot.

**What is verified before anything is installed**

- The download's SHA-256 against the published manifest.
- An **Ed25519 channel signature** over
  `<product>\n<platform>\n<version>\n<file>\n<sha256>\n`, checked against a
  public key compiled into Depot. Write access to this public repository is
  therefore not enough to install code on anybody's machine.
- The version is inside the signed bytes, so a valid old signature cannot be
  replayed to force a downgrade; the filename is inside them too, so a signature
  covering one artefact cannot be presented alongside another from the same
  release.

**Known limits in 0.1.0**

- Depot does not update itself yet. It would have to quit itself mid-install, and
  doing that correctly needs a helper process. Rebuild it from source, or
  download it from the store page.
- Android is a separate build, not in this release.

products.name: Drift
products.tagline: The gap between what you said mattered and where the time went
products.description:
You write down what matters. Then you spend three weeks on something else. Drift puts both halves on one screen: your stated priorities on a Now / Next / Later / Parked board, against where your attention measurably went — and names the gap.

The attention half is not self-reported, which is the point. Drift reads the transcripts your AI coding sessions already leave on disk and derives what you actually worked on from them. Nothing is typed in twice and nothing is flattering.

A Reports inbox treats your Desktop as mail: generated reports arrive, and it headlines how long each one has gone unopened. The ones you never read are the most useful thing on that screen.

It reads local session transcripts from your home directory. Nothing is uploaded — there is no server and no account — but that is the data it works from, so it is worth knowing before you run it.

products.name: Foundry
products.tagline: Finds every app you had an AI build, and what it was built from
products.description:
Build enough small tools and you lose track of them. Foundry is the registry: it scans the places apps actually end up, identifies the ones that are yours, and shows each with its version, its size, what it was built with, and links straight to its source repository and its runtime data folder.

Launch, reveal in Finder, or open the repo in a terminal. Favourites and ordering are yours to set and are remembered.

It identifies apps by bundle identifier prefix rather than by guessing. A heuristic like "small and unsigned" would sweep in half of Applications; an allowlist finds the things you made and nothing else. Extra roots and extra identifiers are settings, so an app in an unusual place can be added without a rebuild.

A caveat worth stating plainly: Foundry resolves each app to its source repository through a table of conventions — where repos live, how project folders are named. Those conventions are the author's. On a machine laid out differently it will still find and launch your apps, but the repo and runtime links will come up empty until you point its extra-roots setting at the right places.

products.name: Harbor
products.tagline: Every listening port on your machine, and a button to kill it
products.description:
"Port 3000 is already in use" — by what, started from where, and how long ago? Harbor answers that as a card per listening port: the port, a guess at the service (Vite dev server, PostgreSQL), the process, its uptime, and the project folder it was launched from.

Two clicks to kill, or to force it. A **Free it** box takes a port number and clears whatever is holding it. A Projects view groups ports by repository root, so you can see that three of them belong to the same checkout. A Log records ports appearing, disappearing and being signalled.

It rescans only while the window is in front. There is no daemon and nothing runs when the app is closed.

A process that ignores a polite shutdown is reported rather than assumed dead — Harbor rescans after signalling and tells you it ignored SIGTERM instead of pretending it worked.

products.name: Lair
products.tagline: A project tracker that runs on your own machine
products.description:
Epics, stories, bugs and tech debt across every project, in a board that opens instantly and works with no network.

There is no server and no account. The whole database is one SQLite file in your home directory, which means it is yours, it is greppable, and backing it up is copying a file.

Four themes including a sepia reading mode, tight 2–6dp corners, and a high-contrast vibe for when the room is bright.

macos.notes:
Lair 2.0.1 — the first build published to the release channel.

Until now Lair was installed by a script that overwrote `/Applications/Lair.app`
on the machine it was built on. This is the same app, packaged so it can be
handed to somebody else and kept current by Depot.

**Installing**

- Unzip and drag to Applications, or let [Depot](../depot/) do it — Depot
  replaces the bundle atomically and quits a running copy first, which a manual
  drag does not.
- Your board lives in `~/.undercurrent/lair/db/lair.db` and is untouched by an
  update. It is one SQLite file: copying it is a backup.

**First launch**

This build is ad-hoc signed rather than notarised, so macOS asks once. Open
**System Settings → Privacy & Security** and click **Open Anyway**. Installing
through Depot skips this entirely — a Depot install carries no quarantine flag.

**Note on size**

180 MB unpacked. Lair is a Compose Desktop app and ships its own Java runtime, so
the download is what it is. Nothing is downloaded at first run.

products.name: Laterbase
products.tagline: Park the good idea that would have derailed your afternoon
products.description:
Mid-task, a better idea arrives. Chasing it costs the afternoon; dropping it loses the idea. Laterbase takes the third option: park it with enough detail that it is still actionable in three weeks, and get back to work.

A parked excursion is not a one-line note. It carries the requirements you would have had to rediscover — what it is for, what it depends on, what finishing looks like — as a checklist an AI session can execute from and tick off as it goes. A board shows what is parked, what is running and what is done; a calendar shows how long each one actually took against what you thought.

Parking works from wherever you already are. The `lb` command parks and ticks from a terminal or an AI session, and the app is a view over the same store, so nothing has to be re-entered to be visible.

Sync is end-to-end sealed. The board replicates through a plain object store — segments are encrypted with a key that stays in the keychain, so the storage provider holds ciphertext and nothing else. Because every write has been in an operation log from the first one, adding a second device needs no migration.

products.name: Necessary Actions
products.tagline: The queue of things only a person can do
products.description:
Automation stops at the things that need a human: create the account, click Allow, paste the secret, approve the charge, read the SMS code, plug in the device. Those pile up invisibly and block work that is otherwise finished.

Necessary Actions is one queue for them, shared across everything running on the machine. Each entry carries literal steps in order — the button to press, the exact value, the URL — an estimate, what it unblocks, and how to hand control back when it is done.

The point is the handback. An action that gets completed and then sits there has saved nobody any time, so every entry records how to resume whatever was waiting on it.

products.name: Nixonizer
products.tagline: Every recorded call, with the transcript and the screenshots back in sync
products.description:
A recorded call leaves a pile of separate things: an audio file, a transcript in several stages, a report, and the screenshots you took while it was happening. Separately they are nearly useless — the screenshot that explains a sentence is forty files away from it. Nixonizer indexes them as one recording and plays it back together: the transcript follows the audio, and each screenshot surfaces at the moment it stops being a mystery.

Screenshots are matched to the call by capture time, which is why the start time is editable and re-matchable — a clock that was off by a minute puts every image in the wrong place. Duplicates are detected and only ever moved on an explicit re-match, never as a side effect of something else.

Anything can be dropped onto a recording — files, images, folders, links — and stays with it. **Deeper analysis with Claude** opens a dedicated session seeded with the call's context, which writes a report and registers it back onto the recording, so the analysis lives beside what it was about rather than in a chat log.

It does not own the recordings. The transcriber that produced them keeps its folders and its rebuild rules, and Nixonizer keeps your state — tags, stars, notes, titles, play position, attachments — in its own store, so nothing you added is at risk when a report is rebuilt.

products.name: PitchRoom
products.tagline: One shelf for every deck and one-pager you send out
products.description:
Outbound documents scatter — a build directory, a Drive folder, a downloads folder, three near-identical versions and no memory of which one actually went out. PitchRoom indexes them all into one view and is explicit about which is current.

One pointer per document decides what is current, and it is the only thing the app treats as authoritative. Everything else is history, kept and browsable rather than deleted, because the question is usually "what did I send in August" rather than "what is newest".

A caveat worth stating plainly: the folders PitchRoom looks in are hardcoded to one machine's layout — a specific Drive mount, a specific build directory, the Desktop. It launches anywhere and, until those paths are changed in the source, shows nothing. It is published because it is a small, readable example of the pattern, not because it is ready to be useful to you.

products.name: Tunnel Bore
products.tagline: Hand long jobs to a machine that never sleeps, without being rude about it
products.description:
A laptop is the wrong place to run something that takes four hours. Tunnel Bore joins a roaming Mac to an always-on machine over a self-hosted WireGuard overlay, and gives you a queue there that does not care whether the lid is open.

`bore push` hands a job to the node. `bore status` is the fleet on one screen, cached so it still tells you something when the node is unreachable. `bore drain` says you are going offline on purpose, which is different from having vanished. `bore doctor` says what is wired and what is not, in the order you should fix it.

**The borrowed-machine part is the point.** The always-on node is often a household PC somebody else games on. A courtesy warden watches for that and yields — the queue pauses itself rather than competing for a GPU, and resumes when the machine is idle again. It detects rather than asks, because a tool that needs permission every time gets turned off.

Secrets never rest on the node. Anything stored there is sealed to a public key whose private half stays in the Mac's keychain, so a node that is lost or reinstalled leaks nothing. The node kit ships the WireGuard generator, the sealed vault and the setup steps for both Linux and Windows.

products.name: WhatsApp Developer Studio
products.tagline: Bring up a WhatsApp pager channel without guessing at Meta's rules
products.description:
Getting a WhatsApp Business number to the point where it can page a human on call is two dozen steps across four Meta surfaces, and the failure mode is discovering on the night it matters that a template was never approved. This is the desk for that work: the checklist, the identifiers, the console and the load tests in one place, each step recorded as it lands.

**Accounts** holds every id you accumulate — developer login, portfolio, app, business account, phone-number ids, test recipients — each with its own journal, because the id is never the hard part to find again; the reason you chose it is. **Console** sends in mock, test or live mode, simulates inbound messages, previews what a page looks like on each channel, and keeps the message and webhook logs. The mock API and webhook receiver run as managed helpers, so the whole loop can be exercised before a real number exists.

**Load Lab** runs named scenarios against that private mock under Meta's published limits, and records the verdict rather than leaving it in a terminal you closed.

It is built for a pager ladder, not a chat app: detail stays on the secure channel, and every other rung carries a content-free page that sends the recipient back to it. **Channels** makes that explicit — a ceiling per channel for what class of payload may cross it, and an audit entry whenever a ceiling moves.

Credentials live in the macOS Keychain. Nothing secret is written to the app's database.
